Article Title: Kelly Clarkson will perform at a Miami charity gala on November 7 as the event marks more than $50 million raised and over 9,000 wishes granted to children with critical illnesses across South Florida
Article Text:
Kelly Clarkson (Instagram)

A night built around hope

What the gala has achieved

Kelly Clarkson’s role

How the evening unfolds

Why the mission matters

Kelly Clarkson will perform at the 31st annual InterContinental Miami Make-A-Wish Ball on November 7, 2026, bringing her chart-topping hits to a night built around hope, philanthropy and the power of a wish. The event, which has raised more than $50 million over the past 30 years, has helped grant the wishes of more than 9,000 children facing critical illnesses across Southern Florida, according to the gala’s official site and Good Housekeeping.Clarkson’s performance will be a private concert featuring songs including 'Because of You', 'Stronger' and her new single 'I’d Be Lyin'. The announcement, shared on Instagram on October 23, drew an enthusiastic response from fans of 'The Voice', where Clarkson is currently a coach on season 30.The InterContinental Miami Make-A-Wish Ball is an annual fundraiser for Make-A-Wish Southern Florida, whose mission is to create life-changing wishes for children with critical illnesses. This year’s theme, the Crystal Castle, promises an evening of shimmering ice, celestial beauty and enchantment set within a snowy Celestine Peaks landscape.The ball is more than a dinner and a performance. It is a celebration of the wishes that have already been granted and a fundraising effort to ensure that every eligible child in the region can have their own wish fulfilled.The event’s organisers describe a wish as a powerful force, one that delivers hope, inspires courage and transforms lives. That framing is central to the gala’s identity, which has grown from a local fundraiser into one of Miami’s most recognisable philanthropic nights.Over the past 30 years, the InterContinental Miami Make-A-Wish Ball has raised more than $50 million. That money has helped grant the wishes of more than 9,000 children facing critical illnesses throughout Southern Florida.Those numbers represent more than a fundraising milestone. Each wish granted is a moment of joy, escape or connection for a child and family navigating an illness that can dominate every part of daily life.The gala’s legacy is built on that accumulation of individual moments. Thirty years of dinners, auctions, performances and donations have added up to a body of work that continues to shape how the community supports its most vulnerable young people.Clarkson’s involvement brings a major cultural draw to the evening. The singer will perform a private concert of her biggest hits, giving guests a chance to hear songs that have defined her career in an intimate setting.Her connection to the cause goes beyond the performance itself. By lending her voice and star power to the gala, Clarkson helps amplify the message that a wish can be a turning point for a child facing a critical illness.The announcement of her performance came just days before she spoke about The Kelly Clarkson Show winning five Daytime Emmy Awards. The show ended in August after seven seasons, and Clarkson shared a heartfelt message thanking the team behind it.The ball begins at 6:30 pm with a reception and silent auction, followed by dinner, performances and the live auction. The after-party runs from midnight to 3 am, extending the night well beyond the formal program.The event is black tie, with complimentary valet parking at the InterContinental Miami at 100 Chopin Plaza. Guests are invited to step into the Crystal Castle theme, which promises a journey of fantasy, mystery and extraordinary philanthropy.The combination of a high-profile performer, an immersive theme and a live auction is part of what has made the gala a fixture on Miami’s social calendar. It is designed to raise both money and awareness for Make-A-Wish Southern Florida’s ongoing work.Make-A-Wish Southern Florida’s work is grounded in the idea that a wish can change how a child and family experience illness. The organisation’s focus is not only on granting wishes but on ensuring that every eligible child has the chance to have one.The gala’s 31st year is a reminder of how much can be accomplished when a community commits to a cause over time. More than $50 million raised and more than 9,000 wishes granted represent decades of effort from donors, volunteers, staff and supporters.With Kelly Clarkson headlining the night, the 2026 ball aims to build on that legacy. The performance is a celebration of what has been achieved, and a signal that the work of granting wishes is far from over.
Article Summary: Kelly Clarkson will perform at the 31st annual InterContinental Miami Make-A- Wish Ball on November 7, 2026. Her performance will be a private concert featuring songs including 'Because of You', 'Stronger' and her new single 'I’d Be Lyin' The event has raised more than $50 million over the past 30 years, and helped grant the wishes of more than 9,000 children.

Article Title: In 2016, Jim Carrey bought a Maui oceanfront retreat for $16.5 million; after listing it for $35 million in October 2026, he found a buyer within weeks, though the final sale price is not yet known
Article Text:
The great room features soaring ceilings, exposed wooden trusses and seamless access to a covered outdoor lanai.

Terminates 10 years of ownership

Two houses with a view of the Pacific

A resort at home

A more quiet life away from Hollywood

Another major real estate exit

For nearly a decade, Jim Carrey’s Hawaiian retreat provided him with something Hollywood rarely could — privacy, solitude and the calming presence of the Pacific Ocean. The property is located on just under an acre of prime beachfront land on Maui and is designed to blur the lines between indoor living and the tropical landscape outside. Now the actor looks ready to let go of the stunning estate. Carrey has already sold the property he listed in October 2026 for $35 million, another significant real estate move for the Hollywood star as he enters a new chapter of his personal life.As per Realtor report, Carrey purchased the oceanfront property in 2016 for $16.5 million, said the realtor. His current asking price is $35 million, more than double what he originally paid for it. The Realtor’s property records show that the home is in pending status, which means a buyer is in place, but the amount of the sale has not been released.The property sits on nearly an acre of beachfront land at Keawakapu Beach where South Kihei Road meets the Wailea resort area. The property has approximately 170 feet of ocean frontage, with a wide green lawn and tall coconut palms between the houses and the shore.The estate was designed by architecture firm Ike Kligerman Barkley, with the goal of weaving traditional Hawaiian influences into a sprawling contemporary retreat, states a report by James Edition.Architectural details include thatched roofing, Douglas fir framing, and woven bamboo finishes.The property is 4,717 square feet and was built in 2002, and is spread out over two separate buildings. The main residence has the primary living areas and a main bedroom suite, while a second building provides independent accommodation for guests.The main house has three bedrooms in total across the accommodation of the estate and the guest structure has two further bedrooms with their own bathrooms. The property also has four and a half bathrooms.One of the characteristics is the great room with high ceilings and wooden trusses that create the airy atmosphere. Big openings connect the interiors to a covered stone lanai, allowing residents to flow easily between the inside and outside.The chef's kitchen has two oversized islands, white cabinetry and premium appliances, according to Realtor. The master suite has another unique feature: a swinging bed and floor-to-ceiling windows, and its bathroom features a statement soaking tub and dual vanities.The outdoor spaces are the estate’s biggest attractions. A freeform swimming pool snakes through natural rock formations in between the two buildings. The design features a hidden grotto, a water slide, a shallow lounging ledge and an elevated spa.According to The James Edition, one of the property’s most valuable features is its generous beachfront setting. Its placement allows both buildings to have ocean views and still have a good stretch of landscaped grounds between the residences and the sand.The listing is with Hawaii Life’s Blake Hill and the estate is being sold fully furnished and in excellent condition. "It is an unusual offering in the luxury property market of Maui with its combination of architectural design, privacy and direct beach access."Carrey's relationship with Maui reflects a broader shift in his lifestyle over the past decade. The actor gradually slipped from the limelight into a more private existence after becoming one of Hollywood's most recognizable comedy stars in 1994 with films such as Ace Ventura: Pet Detective, The Mask and Dumb and Dumber.James Edition notes that his island routine has mostly involved reading, writing, walking, painting and sketching. Carrey has also expressed his desire to retire from acting and lead a quieter life away from the demands of the entertainment industry.His private life, too, has entered a new phase. The actor recently wed his longtime love, Min Ah, in an intimate Los Angeles ceremony, Realtor reports. The couple have kept their relationship largely private, making the development a major milestone.Carrey’s listing in Maui comes after he sold his longtime estate in Brentwood, Los Angeles. The two-acre property was purchased in 1994 for $3.8 million and was first listed in February 2023 for $28.9 million.According to Realtor, however, it was difficult to find a buyer. After several price cuts, the home finally sold in 2024 for $17 million,Carrey now has a buyer for his Hawaiian retreat and appears to be letting go of another major property. It’s not clear whether he plans to have a home elsewhere in Hawaii or to establish his business in California. Its new owner has a new chapter ahead for the Maui estate, though the final sale price has not been disclosed.Images Courtesy: Instagram/jimcarrey and Realtor
Article Summary: Carrey purchased the oceanfront property in 2016 for $16.5 million. His current asking price is $35 million, more than double what he originally paid for it. The property is 4,717 square feet and was built in 2002. The main residence has the primary living areas and a main bedroom suite, while a second building provides independent accommodation for guests.

Article Title: Built in 1904 for a Stanford Greek professor, Palo Alto’s columned Squire House is a state historic landmark; last sold in 1999, the nearly 8,400-sq-ft estate with a pool and guest house is listed for
Article Text:
Built for a man fascinated by the classics

The campaign that saved the mansion

What the nearly $20 million estate offers

A century-old mansion in California, once threatened with demolition and later saved through a community-led preservation campaign, has returned to the property market with an asking price of nearly $20 million. The historic Squire House, a white-columned Neoclassical estate on Palo Alto’s University Avenue, is listed for $19.988 million. It is the first time the property has been offered for sale since it last changed hands in 1999, according to a report by The Almanac.Built in 1904 for John Adams Squire and his wife, Georgiana, the mansion stands on a nearly one-acre property in the city’s Crescent Park neighbourhood. The main residence spans 7,794 square feet, while a separate 600-square-foot guest house brings the total built-up area to approximately 8,394 square feet. The estate also includes landscaped gardens, a swimming pool and a terrace with a fireplace, according to the property's listing by DeLeon Realty.But the house's significance extends beyond its size and price. Known for its grand two-storey portico and Ionic columns, it is recognised as California Historical Landmark No. 857 and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Its survival helped galvanise Palo Alto's historic-preservation movement.Squire, who lived from 1857 to 1930, came to Palo Alto in 1891 when he enrolled at Stanford University for advanced studies in classics. Originally from Massachusetts, he was the son of a wealthy meat packer whose business interests were eventually sold to the Swift company. However, Squire was more interested in ancient languages and teaching than in the family business. He had earlier tutored students in Latin and Greek at the San Jose Normal School, now San Jose State University, and College of the Pacific. After moving to Palo Alto, he and Georgiana became part of the city's early community, among its first 35 households.The couple initially lived in a smaller home on Emerson Street before commissioning San Francisco architect T. Paterson Ross to design their University Avenue residence. Builder George W. Mosher constructed the house in 1904. The architecture reflected Squire's academic interests. Designed in the Roman Classic Revival style, the mansion drew inspiration from ancient Greek and Roman buildings. Its imposing two-storey entrance features a triangular pediment supported by Ionic columns, while the interiors retain details such as quarter-sawn oak floors, leaded-glass windows, oak panelling, pocket doors and elaborate woodwork.The living room has a fireplace with a mahogany mantel, while the dining room features oak panelling and a built-in sideboard. One of the more unusual details of the property is its attic, which Squire's three daughters reportedly used as a roller-skating rink while growing up. The house also survived the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. Although two chimneys collapsed, its columns and exterior remained standing, according to historical accounts cited by The Almanac.The Squire family continued to occupy the property until Georgiana's death in 1959. By the early 1970s, however, the mansion faced a very different future. Its owner planned to sell the land to a buyer who intended to demolish the house and construct four homes on the site. The proposal prompted opposition from neighbours and local preservationists. The Palo Alto Historical Association organised a Save the Squire House Committee, while residents rallied to prevent the loss of one of the city's most recognisable buildings.The city purchased the property and held it for a year, giving preservation advocates time to raise funds. The campaign collected $90,000, with local Girl Scouts even organising bake sales to contribute to the effort. The city separately spent $118,000 on structural improvements before selling the mansion to a private buyer for $135,000. The sale came with a façade easement, which protects the home's exterior and grounds and requires city approval for changes. The preservation effort helped build momentum for wider protections of historic buildings across Palo Alto.The Squire House was registered as California Historical Landmark No. 857 on October 31, 1972. The city also adopted its Historic Preservation Ordinance in 1979 and established a Historic Resources Board to review proposed changes to designated properties.More than 120 years after its construction, the mansion combines its historic exterior with modern luxury features. The current listing describes a five-bedroom property with six full bathrooms and a half-bath, formal living and dining spaces, a private study and a marble kitchen.A finished lower level includes a game room and theatre, while an additional top-floor space can be used for work or recreation. Outside, the grounds feature sweeping lawns, a swimming pool and a trellis-covered terrace with a fireplace. The separate one-bedroom guest house provides additional accommodation.The property is being marketed at $19,988,000, according to the real estate listing. Its main residence accounts for 7,794 square feet, with the guest house adding another 600 square feet.
Article Summary: Built in 1904 for John Adams Squire and his wife, Georgiana, the mansion stands on a nearly one-acre property in the city’s Crescent Park neighbourhood. The main residence spans 7,794 square feet, while a separate 600-square-foot guest house brings the total built-up area to approximately 8,394 square feet.

Article Title: A Louisiana divorce court ordered a wife to pay her former husband $205,000 after a fight over shared property and spending on a new partner; on appeal, the ruling flipped and the husband was ordered
Article Text:
Representative image

What the trial court decided

Why the appeal changed everything

The role of community property

Why spending on a new partner matters

What the reversal means practically

A cautionary divorce story

A Louisiana divorce dispute that began with a fight over shared property and money spent on a new partner has ended in a dramatic legal reversal. According to the Louisiana Third Circuit Court of Appeal decision published by Justia U.S. Law, a trial court initially ordered a wife to pay her former husband $205,000 after finding that she had mishandled community assets and spent money connected with a new relationship. On appeal, however, the appellate court rejected key parts of that outcome and instead ordered the husband to pay her $176,800.The case is a reminder that divorce judgments are not always final in the way people expect. In Louisiana, where marital property is generally treated as community property, courts must sort out what belongs to each former spouse, how debts should be allocated, and whether one party owes the other an equalizing payment. The appellate court’s decision shows how a trial judge’s interpretation of the evidence, the timing of spending, and the legal classification of assets can completely change who walks away owing money.At the trial level, the dispute centered on the division of property acquired during the marriage and certain expenditures made after the relationship broke down. The husband argued that the wife had improperly used or disposed of shared assets, including spending connected to a new partner.The trial court accepted that position in material part and entered a judgment requiring the wife to pay him $205,000.That kind of ruling can feel especially personal because it goes beyond simply dividing a house, retirement account, or bank balance. It asks whether one spouse depleted, wasted, or unfairly claimed property that legally belonged to both of them. Louisiana law treats property acquired during marriage as community property unless it falls into a separate category, such as property owned before marriage, inherited property, or property received individually as a gift.The trial court’s decision therefore reflected a conclusion that the wife had received more than her fair share of the marital estate, or had caused the community to lose value in a way that justified a monetary payment to the husband. The $205,000 figure was intended to correct that perceived imbalance.The wife challenged the ruling, and the Third Circuit Court of Appeal reviewed whether the trial court had properly applied Louisiana’s community-property rules and whether its findings were supported by the evidence. The appellate court ultimately reached a different conclusion. Rather than leaving the husband with a $205,000 award, it reversed the judgment and ordered him to pay the wife $176,800.That is not a small adjustment. It is a swing of $381,800 in the parties’ relative positions. The wife went from being ordered to pay a substantial sum to receiving one herself. The reversal indicates that the appellate court found legal or factual errors in the way the trial court classified, valued, or allocated the property and spending at issue.Appeals do not usually give a higher court permission to simply substitute its own preferences for those of the trial judge. In contrast, if the appellate court finds that the trial court misapplied the law or applied the wrong legal standard or made findings that are not supported by sufficient evidence in the record, it may reverse or modify the judgment. That appears to be what happened here.Louisiana is a community-property state, which means assets and debts acquired during the marriage are generally owned by both spouses. When a marriage ends, the court’s task is to divide the community estate so that each spouse receives property of equal net value. If one spouse receives assets worth more than the other, the court can order an equalizing payment.That principle matters because the dispute was not merely about who spent money on whom. It was about whether particular spending reduced the community estate, whether it was properly charged to one spouse, and whether the final division reflected the true value of what each party received. A court may allocate an asset or liability entirely to one spouse, divide it between them, or order a payment to balance the overall result.In this case, the appellate court’s decision suggests that the trial court’s accounting did not withstand scrutiny. The wife’s spending on a new partner may have been relevant to the dispute, but relevance alone does not automatically determine the financial outcome. The court still had to decide whether the money was community property, whether it was dissipated, how it should be valued, and what offset, if any, was legally appropriate.Money spent during or after a separation can become a flashpoint in divorce litigation. A spouse may contend that community funds paid for travel, gifts, housing, or a new relationship and should be considered a depletion of marital assets. The other spouse might say the money was from separate property, was spent after the community ended, or was lawful personal spending.Louisiana law distinguishes between community and separate property. Assets acquired before marriage, after the divorce petition is filed, or through inheritance or individual gift are generally separate property. That distinction can be decisive when a court evaluates whether spending should affect the division of the marital estate.The appellate ruling does not mean that a spouse can freely spend shared money on a new relationship without consequences. It means that the legal analysis must be precise. A trial court must identify the source of the funds, the timing of the spending, the value of the property involved, and the proper remedy before ordering one former spouse to compensate the other.For the wife, the appeal transformed a major financial liability into a substantial recovery. Instead of paying $205,000, she is now positioned to receive $176,800 from her former husband, according to the appellate decision.For the husband, the result is a costly reminder that winning at trial does not guarantee winning on appeal. The appellate court’s willingness to reverse the financial direction of the case shows that the record, the legal classification of assets, and the calculation of offsets were central to the dispute.For anyone going through a divorce in Louisiana, the broader lesson is practical: keep clear records of major purchases, transfers, debts, and payments made during the marriage and after separation. Community-property disputes often turn on documentation, valuation, and timing rather than on who behaved worse emotionally.This case illustrates how quickly a divorce can become a high-stakes financial accounting exercise. A fight over a new partner may capture attention, but the court’s final decision depended on established rules about marital property, evidence, and the division of assets.The $205,000 trial-court award and the $176,800 appellate award represent two very different versions of fairness. The Louisiana Third Circuit’s reversal shows that the version that survives is the one supported by the law and the evidence, not necessarily the one that seemed persuasive at first.
Article Summary: A Louisiana divorce dispute that began with a fight over shared property and money spent on a new partner has ended in a dramatic legal reversal. A trial court initially ordered a wife to pay her former husband $205,000 after finding that she had mishandled community assets. On appeal, however, the appellate court rejected key parts of that outcome and instead ordered the husband to pay the wife $176,800.

Article Title: Jo Nabuurs lost his wedding ring while threshing grain on his family’s Dutch farm in the winter of 1942 or 1943; 83 years later, a man with a metal detector found it and returned it to his son, refusi
Article Text:
A man searching the area with a metal detector found the missing ring (AI image)

Son recognises father's wedding ring

Family receives ring in good condition

A wedding ring that went missing on a Dutch farm during World War II has finally returned to its owner's family after 83 years. The ring belonged to Jo Nabuurs, who lost it while threshing grain behind his family farm in the village of Odiliapeel in the winter of 1942 or 1943. He searched for it at the time but never managed to find it.Nabuurs had married in 1941, just a year or two before losing the ring. Despite his efforts to recover it, the ring remained buried on the farmland for decades. He later passed away without getting it back.According to Dutch broadcaster NOS, now, more than eight decades later, a man searching the area with a metal detector has found the missing ring. He discovered it about 20 centimetres below the ground in Odiliapeel, a village in the Dutch province of North Brabant.The discovery eventually reached Jo Nabuurs' family through a relative who lives near their former home. After hearing about the find, the relative contacted Jo's son, Bert Nabuurs, and told him that someone would be visiting him.The man who found the ring then personally brought it back to the family. Bert said he was surprised by the unexpected discovery, especially because the ring had been missing for so long. He also offered the finder a reward, but the man refused to accept any payment.For Bert, the return of the ring brought back memories of his father and the story of how the family had lost the wedding jewellery.He told Dutch broadcaster DTV Nieuws that he had heard about the missing ring from his father. However, he had never seen him wearing it. Since Jo had lost the ring before Bert could remember, he had known his father only without a wedding band on his ring finger."My father sometimes told me that he had lost his ring," Bert said, as reported by Dutch broadcaster NOS.Although the ring had spent more than eight decades underground, the family had little difficulty establishing who it belonged to. Its inside carried an engraving of Jo and his wife's wedding date.This detail confirmed that the ring was the same one Jo had lost while working behind the farm. The engraved date also connected the recovered object directly to his parents' marriage in 1941.Bert said the family was delighted that the ring had finally been found. His brothers and sisters were particularly happy about its return after so many years. "My brothers and sisters think it's fantastic that the ring has been found," he said.Bert also said he had asked whether the man wanted a reward for finding and returning the family heirloom. However, the finder declined the offer. "I thought it was quite unusual. I even asked whether he wanted a reward, but he didn't."Apart from the engraved wedding date, the condition of the ring was another detail that pleased the family. Despite spending 83 years buried underground, it had remained in good condition.Bert said the ring had always been kept dry, which helped explain why it had survived so well. "The ring is still in good condition. It has always been kept dry," he said.The family was happy to have the ring back, even though Jo was no longer alive to see its return. For his children, the discovery brought back an object connected to their parents' marriage and a story their father had occasionally shared with them.
Article Summary: ring belonged to Jo Nabuurs, who lost it while threshing grain behind his family farm in the village of Odiliapeel. He searched for it at the time but never managed to find it. Despite his efforts to recover it, the ring remained buried on the farmland for decades. Now, more than eight decades later, a man searching the area with a metal detector has found it.

Article Title: Utah millionaire father of seven built a 300-acre doomsday compound stocked with food, weapons and supplies to shelter 200 people if civilisation collapses; property now doubles as a TV filming locati
Article Text: If you've been watching Homestead on your phones and TVs, beware that there is more of where it's coming from. Jayson Orvis, the author of the post-apocalyptic thriller, has a 300-acre doomsday compound matching the theme, according to a report from PEOPLE. Orvis has spent more than a decade on transforming the property located in Bountiful, Utah, into a self-supporting sanctuary which can shelter 200 people in the event of a civilisation-ending catastrophe. The property, home to the multimillionaire, his wife and three of his seven kids comes with a complete armoury, a machine shop, greenhouses, butchery and a massive storeroom filled with everything from medical textbooks to portable radios and leather-working tools.The location is also the set for his similar themed TV show, Angel Studios' 'Homestead: The Series', which recently returned for Season 2. The 57-year-old entrepreneur's property also boasts a "food forest" that grows fruits and vegetables without pesticides or synthetic fertilisers. “We have more asparagus and raspberries than we can pick,” he told PEOPLE. “We don’t have cattle, but we have wild deer, turkey, elk, goats, rabbits and chickens — natural meat that lives a full life and then we harvest it,” he added.Orvis is admittedly very interested in survival amid catastrophe but he believes that doomsday prepping can be less "dark, nihilistic, and antisocial." He co-wrote the post-apocalyptic thriller Black Autumn book series that was spun off into the feature film Homestead and now a TV series.The only thing that Orvis' property doesn't have is a massive blast-resistant underground concrete bunker which is the first thing secured by billionaires like Mark Zuckerberg in preparations for the end times. But the idea of relying on a fortified bunker to survive the end of civilisation isn't thinking big enough, he said to the outlet. “It’s like a weird prepper idea from the Cold War,” he said. “If you’re going to be right at ground zero [it might make sense] — but up here, you don’t need to bury yourself in the ground. And even if you did, what are you gonna have once you emerge from the ground?”If the apocalypse arrives and the society collapses, Orvis and his group of family, friends, medical experts, master gardeners, beekeepers, Navy SEALs, and even a few Afghan refugee commandos would retreat behind the gates of his compound, with its stockpile of 110,000 pounds of grain, a freshwater well and a massive array of electricity-generating solar panels.“We’ll be super well defended and we’ll also do the best we can to share and to help our neighbours along,” said Orvis, who calculated that the group could survive “indefinitely” on their cache of supplies and what they can cultivate from the land.Besides preparing for civilisation’s end, Orvis said he was determined to “redefine what preparedness means.” “One would think that it’s every man for themselves, kill or be killed [when society collapses],” Orvis said. “Jeff told me that after having seen what happened in places like Haiti, Iraq and Afghanistan, it isn’t the people with the belt-fed machine guns who survive. It’s the people who bind together and form powerful, strong communities,” he said mentioning his co-writer Jeff Kirkham, a former Green Beret with multiple tours in Afghanistan and Iraq.Orvis made a fortune more than 15 years ago after his credit repair business was acquired by an equity fund. “My dad was a firefighter turned metal fabricator and a prepper,” he said, adding that he wrote his first article for a prepper journal at the age of 15. “I grew up with chickens, bees, rabbits and gardens in the backyard, so preparedness has always been kind of a hobby,” he said.After selling his business in 2010, Orvis began focusing on philanthropic work and soon found himself “called to help” former special forces soldiers, using his social marketing skills to help them launch entrepreneurial ventures like Black Rifle Coffee and the self-reliance website retailer Readyman. This is when he met Kirkham, and the two began brainstorming ideas for their faith-based post-apocalyptic series that now includes 10 books and, said Orvis, has allowed them to tell stories of “high peril and high hope. ”By then, Orvis had already begun transforming his massive property into a paradise for the point of no return. “We had a garden and food storage, but we didn’t have goats, rabbits, chickens and all this,” recalled Orvis’ wife, Pamela, 57. “So Jayson started digging into it. Before long, everything just snowballed and we took it to the next level.”However, despite all his preparedness and plans, Orvis is "pretty damn sure the world isn't going to collapse." “It is possible, but I think the odds are probably sub-2 or 1% in my lifetime,” he said.
Article Summary: Jayson Orvis, the author of the post-apocalyptic thriller Homestead, has a 300-acre doomsday compound matching the theme. Orvis has spent more than a decade on transforming the property located in Bountiful, Utah, into a self- supporting sanctuary. The location is also the set for his similar themed TV show, Angel Studios' 'Homestead: The Series', which recently returned for Season 2.

Article Title: 'You'll know soon enough': Trump's warning on 'destroying' rest of Iran
Article Text:
Trump issued fresh threats to Iran

US President Donald Trump on Thursday (local time) issued a fresh warning to Iran, saying Washington could take further action against the country while signalling that he would prefer to avoid additional destruction. He also asserted that Tehran could not move ahead with its nuclear programme without US approval."I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I’ll have to. You will know soon enough," Trump told reporters at the Oval Office.Additionally, on Iran's nuclear programme, he said, "They're not doing anything without our approval."can it be slightly longer..to add what's latest in iranThis comes as Trump faces mounting pressure over the eight-month-old Iran war following the Republicans' losses in the US midterm elections, with voter dissatisfaction over the conflict and rising fuel prices emerging as factors in the Democratic gains. Before the elections, Trump had repeatedly threatened to resume large-scale strikes against Iran if Tehran failed to agree to a settlement on terms acceptable to Washington. The conflict has also widened beyond Iran, with tensions spilling into the Red Sea amid attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels and retaliatory action by regional forces.The latest developments point to a widening diplomatic gap. Iran has reportedly sent a fresh proposal on its nuclear programme to the US through Qatar, but Tehran has said negotiations would depend on Washington meeting its demands, including lifting sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian assets and paying reparations. The US is reviewing the proposal, even as Trump has kept the option of renewed military action open. Tensions also remain high around Strait of Hormuz.

He also asserted that Tehran could not move ahead with its nuclear programme without US approval. Trump faces mounting pressure over the eight-month-old Iran war following the Republicans' losses in the US midterm elections.

Article Title: Earthquake of magnitude 5.0 jolts China's Xinjiang region
Article Text:
China's Xinjiang hit by 5.0-magnitude earthquake, says NCS

An earthquake of magnitude 5.0 struck China's Xinjiang region at 10:26 pm IST on Thursday, the National Centre for Seismology (NCS) said.According to the NCS, the earthquake was recorded at 22:26 IST.The earthquake's epicentre was located close to the international border between India and China.There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage.
Article Summary: An earthquake of magnitude 5.0 struck China's Xinjiang region at 10:26 pm IST on Thursday. The earthquake's epicentre was located close to the international border between India and China. There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage.

Article Title: Midterm losses, no exits: Marco Rubio rules out quitting, Donald Trump backs Pete Hegseth
Article Text:
File photo - US President Donald Trump speaks during a media conference as Marco Rubio, right, and Pete Hegseth listen

Rubio backs JD Vance for 2028 presidential race

White House rejects reports of Rubio's possible exit

US secretary of state Marco Rubio has dismissed reports that he is considering leaving the Trump administration following the Republican Party's setbacks in the midterm elections, saying that completing President Donald Trump's second term has “always been my plan”.In an interview with The New York Times, Rubio rejected speculation that he might step down ahead of a possible 2028 presidential campaign and declined to discuss his political ambitions.“Working for President Trump until the end of his term has always been my plan,” Rubio said, adding that he did not know where reports about his possible departure had originated.“I love the work I’m doing,” he said. “And plus I always laugh when they say he’s going to leave his job. I go, ‘Which one?’”Rubio, who also serves as Trump's national security adviser, refused to entertain questions about whether he was considering a presidential run in 2028.“I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore,” he told the newspaper in his White House office. “I just won’t do it.”Rubio has previously indicated that he would support Vice President JD Vance if he decided to run for president in 2028.“JD is a very good friend of mine,” Rubio told NBC News in May. “If JD runs for president, I think he’d be a phenomenal candidate. I’ve said publicly, and I’ll say it again, I’ll be the first person to sign up and support him.”However, Vance's post-election assessment on Wednesday included criticism of the administration's approach to the Iran war, its policy on Israel and its messaging on the economy.The vice-president blamed the war with Iran for the Republicans' election setbacks and said voters had turned against the administration's position on Israel and its handling of economic concerns. Trump has closely aligned himself with Israel and dismissed concerns over affordability as a “hoax”.Asked whether he agreed with Vance's assessment, Rubio initially deflected, saying he was not “really involved in domestic politics”.However, Rubio acknowledged the political implications of the Iran war when he appeared alongside Trump at a rally in Kansas on Sunday. Trump praised the secretary of state and joked that he might have to fire him because he had become “too popular”.Explaining his presence at the rally, Rubio said he was travelling with the president as the designated national security official. He also acknowledged Trump's remarks that the war had been a factor in the election results.“Higher prices at the gas pump, I acknowledge, is not like the kind of thing you campaign on and brag about,” Rubio said.However, he defended Trump's decision to take action despite its potential political costs, saying the president “deserves a tremendous amount of credit” for doing what he considered necessary.“Ultimately, that is the price of leadership — is the willingness to do things that may not be politically popular or expedient but are necessary for your country and its long-term future,” he said.The White House and the State Department have also rejected reports that Rubio could leave his position following the Republican setbacks.White House spokesperson Beni Rae Harmony described the reports as a fabricated hoax circulated by anonymous sources, while assistant secretary of state for global public affairs Dylan Johnson called them baseless fake news.The speculation over a possible administration shake-up has also involved defence secretary Pete Hegseth , whose handling of the Iran war has drawn criticism following the election losses.The White House has denied reports that Hegseth and Rubio might leave their positions. Trump told ABC News that he had received calls about Hegseth but had “every intention” of keeping him. He later praised the defence secretary, saying he had “done a fantastic job”.However, Republican Representative Thomas Massie has said he intends to move ahead with an effort to impeach Hegseth, with a resolution expected as early as next week. Hegseth has rejected the effort, describing it as a politically motivated attempt to undermine him.Separately, The Washington Post reported that Trump could be considering replacing General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command.Both have played significant roles in providing guidance on the Iran war.
Article Summary: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has dismissed reports that he is considering leaving the Trump administration following the Republican Party's setbacks in the midterm elections. In an interview with The New York Times, Rubio rejected speculation that he might step down ahead of a possible 2028 presidential campaign. The White House and the State Department have also rejected reports that Rubio could leave his position.

Article Title: Namaste Uncle Sam: Nithya Raman poised to become LA Mayor, as America's top two cities get desi touch
Article Text:
Elected LA mayor Nithya Raman and New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Nithya Raman's background

How Socialists are storming across American cities:

Indian origin winners from the US midterm elections

Nithya Raman stood before supporters at a downtown Los Angeles brewery in June, struggling to hold back tears. The early primary election returns had placed her third in the race for mayor, behind incumbent Karen Bass and reality tv personality Spencer Pratt, and it looked like the end of the road for her. She gave what was almost a concession speech. Her father Venkit Raman, an IITian, comforted campaign workers, telling them her full name Nithya Varsha means 'everlasting monsoon,' and her political life would be replenished soon.It came sooner than anyone expected because after all this is the la la land of Hollywood where plot twists are common. And appropriately too enough considering her husband, Vali Chandrasekaran, is a successful television writer and producer whose credits include 30 Rock and Modern Family. A batch of late ballots that came in took Raman past Pratt to second place, and because Bass did not get 50 per cent of the vote, there would be a run-off election in November. Even then, few gave the 45-year old political tyro, with only six years of experience on the City Council, any chance. Raman herself had once supported Bass, and the 73-year old party stalwart had the backing of the Democratic establishment, including endorsements from Kamala Harris, Nancy Pelosi and Governor Gavin Newsom.She had experience, name recognition, and the advantage of incumbency.What Bass could not quite escape was the perception that Los Angeles is broken and she did not have the toolkit to fix it. The devastating January 2025 Palisades wildfire, which killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes, became a defining political liability. Bass was abroad when the mishap occurred and her handling of the disaster and recovery became a persistent political liability. Raman’s campaign ignited. She offered herself as the candidate of change, promising better housing, improved public services and more accountable government. An urban planner by training, she could talk about the nuts and bolts of city administration rather than simply deliver ideological sermons. On Tuesday night, her persistence paid off, and although the race has not been officially called, she is ahead by 25,000 votes and looks likely to seal the deal. She invited supporters to join her in a dance on Wednesday, the tears in June now forgotten.Raman's victory is more than an extraordinary personal turnaround. It is another major breakthrough for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the left-wing movement that has been steadily challenging the Democratic Party establishment. And for India, it provides an especially striking political subplot: New York and Los Angeles, America's two largest cities, will now be led by mayors of Indian origin, with Zohran Mamdani already in office in New York.What's even more striking: Long before Mamdani and Raman began making their mark in American municipal politics, several prominent Indian nationalists and intellectuals had encountered the country's radical political traditions first hand. Lala Lajpat Rai spent five years in the U.S between 1914 and 1919, establishing the India Home Rule League and publishing the journal Young India in New York. The radical humanist M.N. Roy arrived in the U.S in 1916 as a global itinerant, encountered American radicals and began studying socialism, subsequently moving to Mexico City, where he founded the Communist Party of Mexico in 1919. He later played a foundational role in establishing the Communist Party of India in 1920. B.R. Ambedkar, meanwhile, studied at Columbia University in NYC, encountering some of America's leading liberal and progressive intellectuals, including philosopher John Dewey. And Jayaprakash Narayan spent seven years in America (1922-1929), studying at Berkeley, Iowa, and Wisconsin, where he encountered Marxism and returned to India a committed socialist.All this was at a time socialism was enjoying considerable electoral popularity. In 1912, Socialist Party presidential candidate Eugene Debs won nearly a million votes, then about 6% of the national total. Socialists also held hundreds of municipal offices, including mayoralties. In fact, in the early 1950s Donald Trump’s father Fred Trump clashed with the folk singer Woody Guthrie, an avowed socialist, over racial segregation and housing discrimination in Brooklyn, causing him to write a song -- a scalding takedown of a predatory landlord -- titled “Old Man Trump" who stirred up racial hatred "in the bloodsport of the human heart. "Indeed, even in the modern era, the current upsurge of socialists did not emerge overnight. One of its earliest conspicuous faces was another Indian activist: Kshama Sawant, born in Pune and raised in Mumbai, who won a seat on Seattle's City Council in 2013. A former economics professor and member of Socialist Alternative rather than the DSA, Sawant became a prominent voice for a $15 minimum wage, rent control and taxing the wealthy. Her victory demonstrated that a politician openly identifying with socialism could win in an American city.Bernie Sanders subsequently took the argument national with his presidential campaigns in 2016 and 2020 bringing democratic socialism into mainstream political conversation, particularly among younger Americans frustrated by inequality, expensive healthcare, housing costs and the influence of corporate money. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's (AOC’s) stunning 2018 primary victory over veteran Democrat Joe Crowley gave the movement another national face. The election of Mamdani as New York mayor in 2025 was an even bigger breakthrough. Mamdani defeated Democratic political heavyweight Andrew Cuomo by campaigning on affordable housing, free bus services, universal childcare and a city government that would work for ordinary people.The movement now has a growing presence in municipal government. Besides Mamdani in New York, democratic socialist or DSA-affiliated mayors include Katie Wilson in Seattle, Janeese Lewis George in Washington DC, Emma Mulvaney-Stanak in Burlington, Robert Cantelmo in Ithaca and Eduardo Martinez in Richmond, California. In the mid-terms, six DSA-endorsed candidates have won seats in the House of Representatives: Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York (both backed by Mamdani), Melat Kiros in Colorado, Angela Gonzales-Torres in California, Donavan McKinney in Michigan and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania. DSA members Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib also won re-election.The organisation's own election tracker reported victories across an even wider range of state and local contests, including in Florida, Maryland, Washington, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Vermont. The significance is not simply the number of elected socialists, but their willingness, like in the case of Raman v Bass, to challenge Democratic incumbents and party leadership rather than wait patiently for establishment approval.While their electoral success is undeniable, the jury is still out on their ability to translate ambitious promises of affordable housing, safer streets, better transport and sustainable municipal finances into reality. Governing New York or Seattle or LA is considerably more complicated than winning an election with a catchy slogan. Already, MAGA bros are cranking up right wing fearmongering with Conservative commentators Benny Johnson invoking scenarios of urban 'Armageddon' a favorite Trump theme.For now though the socialists are having their moment in the sun. The MAGA crowd is predicting an apocalypse, the billionaires are checking their property portfolios, and the Democratic establishment is wondering whether it should start taking out membership in the DSA. Raman and Mamdani now have the rather unenviable task of proving that running a city is not quite the same as running against one. In the process, America's urban political landscape is getting a makeover — and this time, the revolution has an Indian accent.
Article Summary: Nithya Raman and Zohran Mamdani are the new mayors of Los Angeles and New York City respectively. Raman's victory is another major breakthrough for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the left-wing movement that has been challenging the Democratic Party establishment.

Article Title: A Scottish wildlife rescuer saved a starving badger cub trapped in a cattle trough, but officials denied his request to keep her; now he is fighting to retain the animal he says cannot survive in the
Article Text:
Rescued from a cattle trough in April, Harriet was nursed back to health by ecologist Graeme Wilson.

From a desperate rescue to an unusual bond

Why the ecologist wants to keep Harriet

Wildlife experts raise concerns

Harriet's future remains uncertain

Images Courtesy: istock and BBC

A chance encounter with a helpless animal has turned into a complicated battle over wildlife protection, rehabilitation and the limits of human intervention. When Scottish ecologist Graeme Wilson rescued a starving badger cub from a cattle trough, he expected to nurse her back to health. Instead, the experience left him convinced that returning her to the wild could put her life in danger. Now, he is fighting for permission to give Harriet a permanent home, despite opposition from wildlife authorities.According to the BBC, Harriet was discovered in April trapped inside a cattle trough, around 100 metres from her sett in the Scottish Borders. Wilson was called to help the young animal and took responsibility for her recovery, gradually nursing her back to health.However, her behaviour soon raised concerns about whether she could survive independently. Given her bottle feeding response and familiarity with humans, Wilson suspected Harriet was hand-reared before her rescue.As reported by The Telegraph, Wilson believes the cub has become accustomed to humans to such an extent that releasing her into the countryside could expose her to serious risks. He fears she might approach people while out walking, potentially placing herself in a dangerous situation.Wilson operates GW Ecology, an independent wildlife rescue and rehabilitation service from his home in Denholm. Alongside caring for injured animals, his work involves ecological surveys to identify protected species at proposed development sites. He also organises bat walks, workshops and educational activities to encourage greater awareness of wildlife conservation.The ecologist applied to NatureScot for an educational licence that would allow him to continue caring for Harriet while helping the public understand badgers and the challenges involved in rehabilitating protected wildlife.However, the application was rejected. NatureScot suggested that Harriet should either be returned to the wild or transferred to a zoo. Wilson believes neither option would adequately address her circumstances. While a release could expose her to injury or death, he fears a conventional zoo environment would leave her isolated and distressed.The disagreement has brought wider questions about the responsibilities involved in wildlife rehabilitation into focus. The BBC reported that the British Wildlife Rehabilitation Council has stressed the specialist nature of caring for wild animals.Paul Reynolds, who chairs the organisation, has highlighted the importance of suitable facilities, species-specific care, veterinary supervision and an understanding of an animal's natural behaviour. The council also distinguishes responsible rehabilitation from keeping wild animals permanently in captivity for educational or personal purposes.According to The Telegraph, the organisation maintains that an animal becoming accustomed to human contact should not automatically be considered grounds for permanent captivity.NatureScot has indicated that discussions with Wilson and other relevant organisations are continuing in an effort to find a practical resolution. The authority has emphasised that Harriet's welfare remains central to its decision-making process. Police Scotland has also been made aware of the situation.Meanwhile, the Scottish SPCA advises people who encounter sick or injured badgers to contact its rescue officers rather than attempting to handle the animals themselves. Young cubs found away from their setts may need help, and frightened or injured badgers may attack.Wilson still wants a safe future for Harriet. Whether that means an exception to the usual rules or another arrangement, the case highlights the difficult balance between individual animal welfare and the principles of wildlife conservation.
Article Summary: Harriet the badger cub was rescued from a cattle trough in April. Ecologist Graeme Wilson nursed her back to health but is now fighting for permission to give her a permanent home. The British Wildlife Rehabilitation Council has stressed the specialist nature of caring for wild animals.

Article Title: A billionaire's Malibu beach project triggered a dispute over allegedly removed sand; now a $2 million beachfront property is being opened to the public
Article Text:
Image: Brian van der Brug/LA Times

Mark Attanasio faced allegations over sand removed from Malibu’s Broad Beach

$2 million beachfront property will be donated for public use

Image: Court Documents

Agreement also requires restoration of the damaged Malibu shoreline

Malibu’s beaches have faced years of erosion and restoration efforts

A dispute over sand removed from one of Malibu’s most exclusive beaches has led billionaire businessman Mark Attanasio to agree to donate a $2 million beachfront property for public use. The Milwaukee Brewers owner faced allegations that his construction team excavated sand from Broad Beach and transported it to his nearby property during development work in 2024. Following an investigation by the California Coastal Commission, Attanasio agreed to return the sand, restore damaged coastal habitat and provide a separate oceanfront parcel for public recreation. The proposed settlement could create a rare new access point along Malibu’s heavily developed coastline.Mark Attanasio, the billionaire owner of the Milwaukee Brewers baseball team, became involved in a dispute after his construction team was accused of excavating sand from Broad Beach in 2024. Workers allegedly used heavy machinery to remove sand from the public shoreline and transport it to his beachfront property as part of a development project. The work prompted a lawsuit and an investigation by the California Coastal Commission.According to the Los Angeles Times, the commission found that the unauthorised excavation had damaged sensitive coastal habitats and partially obstructed public beach access.Rather than settling the dispute through a conventional financial penalty, Attanasio agreed to donate an oceanfront property valued at approximately $2 million. The 5,135-square-foot parcel is located near Big Rock Beach, around 14 miles east of his Broad Beach mansion. It has 70 feet of beachfront frontage and previously contained a three-unit building that was destroyed in the Palisades fire. Attanasio was under contract to purchase the property and agreed to transfer it to a public agency once the sale was completed, according to the Los Angeles Times. The land is intended for recreational use, although specific plans for the site have not yet been determined.The proposed settlement includes more than the beachfront property donation. Attanasio has also agreed to return the excavated sand and repair the coastal habitat affected by the construction work. The excavation reportedly left a large hole in the rocky intertidal zone, an area that provides habitat for marine species including fish and sea stars. California Coastal Commission enforcement counsel Robert Moddelmog said the donation could help address the longstanding difficulty of creating public access along eastern Malibu, where private homes occupy much of the coastline.The dispute comes as Broad Beach continues to face coastal erosion caused by storms and high tides. The stretch is home to expensive beachfront properties owned by celebrities and business figures, making public access and shoreline preservation longstanding concerns. In 2015, residents including Dustin Hoffman, Ray Romano and Pierce Brosnan committed to a $31 million restoration project aimed at replenishing the beach’s sand. Attanasio’s proposed donation could provide another opportunity for public access in an area where beachfront land is rarely made available for recreational use.
Article Summary: Mark Attanasio faced allegations that his construction team excavated sand from Broad Beach and transported it to his nearby property in 2024. The work prompted a lawsuit and an investigation by the California Coastal Commission. The commission found that the unauthorised excavation had damaged sensitive coastal habitats and partially obstructed public beach access. The billionaire owner of the Milwaukee Brewers baseball team has agreed to donate a $2 million beachfront property for public use.

Article Title: 'Nobody got hurt or killed for five months': Trump plays down Iran conflict
Article Text:
Trump has also reiterated his claim that his administration's intervention prevented Iran from developing nuclear weapons

US President Donald Trump Saturday dismissed the ongoing military confrontation with Iran as "not a war", claiming that nobody had been hurt or killed in the five months since the conflict began, even as Washington continues to carry out strikes against Tehran and explore diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East."We made a lot of progress with Iran. We’re taking out more oil now than we were before the war. It’s not a war. It can’t be a war when for five months nobody was hurt, killed, or anything else. It’s not a war," Trump said.His remarks come amid continuing military activity in the region, with the US military carrying out fresh strikes on Iranian air defence systems. Trump described the latest action as "minor" and said it involved limited targets. Iranian state media, meanwhile, reported two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, a strategically important location near the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil shipments.Despite his assertion that the confrontation does not amount to a war, Washington has continued to consider military options against Iran even as diplomatic efforts gather pace. Qatar has been mediating between the two sides, with the country's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani discussing efforts to end the crisis with Trump during a telephone conversation on Friday.According to the Qatari ruler's media office, the discussions focused on reaching "a comprehensive agreement that ends the crisis and achieves security and stability in the region." Qatar and other Gulf countries have faced Iranian attacks during the conflict and are keen to prevent further escalation.Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has held discussions with regional counterparts on a possible resumption of negotiations with Washington. Iran's proposals reportedly include reopening the Strait of Hormuz, setting a timetable for negotiations and addressing its nuclear programme.Trump has also reiterated his claim that his administration's intervention prevented Iran from developing nuclear weapons. In a post on Truth Social, he said the security of Israel and the wider Middle East depended on the US action."Israel and, in fact, the entire Middle East, WOULD NOT EXIST TODAY if I did not stop Iran from having a Nuclear Weapon. Nobody wants to say that, but everybody knows it’s true!" he wrote.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump Saturday dismissed the ongoing military confrontation with Iran as "not a war" He claimed that nobody had been hurt or killed in the five months since the conflict began. His remarks come amid continuing military activity in the region, with the US military carrying out fresh strikes on Iranian air defence systems.

Article Title: Trump to get 'Trumpier' as hardliner Stephen Miller takes charge of White House; what it means for India
Article Text:
Stephen Miller's appointment as White House chief of staff signals that Donald Trump is doubling-down on his domestic agenda.

What does the chief of staff control?

Immigration

What has Miller said about India?

Domestic policy: A more confrontational final two years?

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think Miller's role in shaping policy will lead to stricter enforcement of existing laws? Yes, it likely will No, it likely won't 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The appointment of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff signals that Donald Trump is unlikely to respond to his party's midterm setbacks by moderating his domestic agenda, according to several US media reports.Instead, the US president appears to be placing one of the most uncompromising architects of his America First programme at the centre of White House decision-making as he prepares for two years of confrontation with a Democratic-controlled Congress.Miller, who has been one of Trump's closest advisers since his first presidential campaign in 2016, will replace Susie Wiles, taking over the position on November 9. The appointment comes after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, leaving Trump with a considerably more hostile legislative environment for the remainder of his presidency.The choice is significant because Miller is not simply an immigration hardliner. As deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, he has been involved in shaping the administration's approach to immigration enforcement, federal power, domestic security and other contentious policy areas.His elevation raises an important question: with legislation likely to become harder to push through Congress, will Trump increasingly rely on executive action to pursue his priorities? For India, the implications could extend well beyond immigration, particularly to H-1B visas, skilled-worker mobility and the future of the US-India economic relationship.The White House chief of staff is arguably the most influential unelected official in the US administration. The position does not carry independent constitutional authority, but it offers enormous influence over how the president exercises his powers.The chief of staff effectively acts as the president's gatekeeper, controlling access to the Oval Office, managing senior White House personnel, coordinating policy discussions and determining which issues receive the president's attention.The role also involves coordinating the work of the National Security Council, domestic policy teams, communications staff and other senior advisers. The chief of staff helps translate presidential priorities into government action, resolves competing demands between officials and ensures that departments are working towards the administration's objectives.Importantly, the chief of staff does not directly command cabinet departments or independently make policy. Those powers remain with the president and the relevant department heads.But the person occupying the position can determine how quickly decisions move, which advisers have the president's ear and how aggressively an existing policy is implemented.Former chief of staff Susie Wiles was widely credited with bringing organisational discipline to Trump's White House. Miller, meanwhile, has been the ideological and policy driving force behind several of the administration's most controversial initiatives. CNN reported that Miller's influence had expanded well beyond immigration, covering much wider areas of domestic policy and homeland security. His elevation therefore brings policy formulation and White House management under the same influential figure.Immigration is likely to remain the centrepiece of Miller's agenda.He was instrumental in designing Trump's first-term family separation policy and has subsequently helped develop the mass deportation programme that became a defining feature of the president's second term.His public statements have consistently advocated aggressive enforcement. He has described illegal immigration as an invasion, called for mass deportations and argued for an expansive interpretation of presidential authority to enforce immigration laws. He has also floated suspending habeas corpus to facilitate deportations, a proposal that raises serious constitutional questions.The political significance of his appointment is that Trump's immigration agenda has become increasingly contentious. Democrats have promised investigations into enforcement practices, while concerns about the treatment of migrants and the use of federal agents have attracted considerable scrutiny.Rather than choosing an adviser associated with recalibration, Trump has promoted someone deeply invested in the existing approach. Miller's appointment could therefore mean more executive action, tougher enforcement and attempts to push the limits of presidential authority, even as congressional oversight intensifies.Unlike some other Trump advisers, Miller has not established a prominent public profile as a commentator on India or articulated a comprehensive India-specific policy doctrine. His public record is principally centred on immigration, national sovereignty, border security and the economic interests of American workers.However, these positions have direct implications for India because Indian nationals constitute one of the largest groups of skilled foreign workers in the United States.In fiscal 2025, India-born beneficiaries accounted for approximately 70% of approved H-1B petitions, according to figures cited from US Citizenship and Immigration Services. This makes Indian professionals particularly exposed to changes in the programme.The Trump administration has already introduced a $100,000 payment requirement for certain new H-1B petitions involving workers outside the US, alongside changes to visa selection that favour higher-paid positions.Miller's promotion raises questions about whether the administration will pursue further restrictions. His emphasis on prioritising American workers could translate into greater scrutiny of employers hiring foreign professionals, tighter enforcement and additional barriers for skilled migrants.The consequences would extend to Indian IT companies, American technology firms, universities and thousands of Indian professionals seeking employment in the US.There is also a potential economic consequence. Reuters has reported that restrictions on H-1B visas could encourage American companies to shift more high-value work to their Indian global capability centres rather than relocating employees to the US.Miller's influence is not restricted to immigration. He has been involved in the administration's efforts to reduce the federal workforce, challenge diversity programmes, confront universities and expand federal enforcement powers.His appointment could give these initiatives greater priority during Trump's remaining two years.With Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress, Trump will face investigations, congressional hearings and resistance to his legislative proposals.Miller is a strong advocate of expansive presidential authority.Consequently, the administration could increasingly turn to executive orders, presidential proclamations and administrative actions to advance policies that might otherwise encounter congressional opposition.That approach, however, will face judicial scrutiny and potential legal challenges. The chief of staff cannot insulate the president's decisions from Congress, the courts or constitutional limits.Miller's appointment offers a glimpse of Trump's priorities after the midterm setback: a White House more firmly organised around his ideological agenda, a harder immigration line and greater reliance on presidential power.Miller's ideas about immigration, American jobs and national sovereignty could have a negative impact on millions of Indians whose professional and economic futures are tied to the US.
Article Summary: Stephen Miller's appointment as White House chief of staff signals that Donald Trump is doubling-down on his domestic agenda. The appointment comes after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections. For India, the implications could extend well beyond immigration, particularly to H-1B visas and skilled-worker mobility.

Article Title: The Star Trek actor Chris Pine sued a Brooklyn developer over a $100,000 rental deposit; the actor says a townhouse deal collapsed before a lease was signed
Article Text:
Chris Pine's $100,000 claim over a failed Brooklyn rental deal

Chris Pine challenges rental payments made before a final agreement

Saavedra’s lawyer shares his side of the case

Inside the $14.25 million Brooklyn townhouse

Chris Pine has faced an earlier property-related lawsuit

A look at Pine's property holdings in Los Angeles

Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available reports and court allegations. The Times of India has not independently verified the claims made in the lawsuit.

Actor Chris Pine has become involved in a property dispute in Brooklyn after a proposed rental arrangement for a luxury townhouse failed to reach the contract stage. The Star Trek actor is seeking to recover $100,000 that he says remains with the developer despite the agreement falling apart before a lease was signed. The property, a renovated 19th-century home in the Cobble Hill neighbourhood, had been discussed as a short-term furnished rental. Pine had already transferred money towards the proposed arrangement, but negotiations over the lease did not produce an agreement. The developer's legal representatives have disputed the account presented in the complaint, describing the matter as a private contractual disagreement.According to The Realtor, the disagreement centres on 487 Henry Street, a substantial townhouse in Cobble Hill, Brooklyn. According to the complaint filed in Kings County, Pine began discussing a short-term rental of the property with developer Carlos Saavedra and his company, Eckstrom, in June 2026.The financial arrangements involved three separate payments totalling $125,000. Pine reportedly paid $50,000 as a security deposit, another $50,000 towards the first month's rent and $25,000 as a deposit for his pet.The pet deposit has since been returned. The actor is now seeking the remaining $100,000, which represents the other two payments connected with the proposed tenancy. His lawsuit also seeks damages and reimbursement of legal costs.Pine's complaint describes a disagreement over the wording of the proposed lease. The actor had reportedly made handwritten changes to the standard rental agreement presented by Saavedra, suggesting amendments to the terms before committing to the arrangement.Those proposed changes were not accepted by the developer, according to the filing. The parties subsequently failed to settle on a final version of the lease. An important part of Pine's legal argument is that he never signed a completed rental contract. The complaint maintains that the intended tenancy did not come into existence, as no final agreement was reached and the actor never took possession of the property. It also argues that the planned rental period would not begin under those circumstances.Saavedra and Eckstrom have responded through their attorney, Russell Wolfson, who represents them in the case. Speaking to The Realtor, Wolfson described the dispute as a private contractual matter. He also cautioned against treating the complaint as a complete account of events, pointing out that legal filings generally present the position of the party bringing the case.He said Saavedra was confident the matter would be resolved through the appropriate legal channels.The property at the centre of the dispute is a five-storey residence dating back to the 19th century. Eckstrom undertook an extensive renovation of the building, transforming it into a furnished luxury home with approximately 6,000 square feet of interior space.The townhouse contains five bedrooms and four bathrooms. Its interiors include white oak flooring, marble and quartzite surfaces, alongside facilities that extend beyond the usual residential features.A fitness studio, sauna and cold plunge are among the amenities. The property also has roughly 2,000 square feet of outdoor space, giving it a considerable amount of additional room across its different levels.Reportedly, the fully furnished residence was being offered for rent at $69,500 a month. It was also marketed for sale at $14.25 million, placing it in the upper end of Brooklyn's luxury property market.The Brooklyn dispute is not the first time Pine has been involved in a legal disagreement concerning a residential property. In 2022, the actor's then-neighbour, music attorney Helen Yu, brought a lawsuit over several ficus Benjamina trees planted in the garden of his Los Angeles home. Yu alleged that the trees had invasive roots that were causing damage and other problems on her property.The disagreement continued for several years before the parties reached a settlement. The matter returned to court in December, when Yu asked a judge to enforce the settlement agreement.Away from the Brooklyn townhouse, Pine has also been linked to residential properties in Los Angeles. In 2021, he purchased a three-bedroom bungalow in Valley Village for approximately $1.4 million. Reports at the time indicated that the property was bought for a family member.He also owns a home in the Los Feliz neighbourhood, which he purchased in 2010 from actor Jason Lee. The property has remained part of his reported Los Angeles real estate holdings.Pine's latest legal dispute arose while he was reportedly in New York working on a film project titled The Catch, alongside Emma Stone.
Article Summary: Star Trek actor is seeking to recover $100,000 that he says remains with the developer despite the agreement falling apart before a lease was signed. The property, a renovated 19th-century home in the Cobble Hill neighbourhood, had been discussed as a short-term furnished rental. The developer's legal representatives have disputed the account presented in the complaint.

The court allowed more claims

Why the damages were reduced

The Texas Court of Appeals has upheld a finding that a refinery company was grossly negligent in the asbestos-related death of a former worker, but reduced his family's damages award from $325,000 to $200,000. In its November 5 ruling, the court also allowed the family to pursue additional claims against the company, sending them back for further proceedings.According to case details on Justia , The case concerns Louie Scudder, who worked at the La Gloria refinery in Tyler, Texas, for a total of 38 years. He first joined the refinery in 1958, left in 1964 and returned in 1966, continuing until 1998. He was diagnosed with mesothelioma in November 2019 and died on June 25, 2022, aged 83.His family alleged that years of exposure to asbestos at the refinery caused his illness and death. His son, Carl Christian Scudder, filed a lawsuit against Tyler MD Holdings LLC, the successor-in-interest to Tyler Holding Company, formerly known as La Gloria Oil and Gas Company.A jury found that asbestos fibres from the refinery had caused Scudder's illness and death. It also held the company grossly negligent and awarded his family $325,000 in exemplary damages.The company challenged the verdict, arguing that the evidence did not establish that Scudder's exposure at the refinery had caused his illness.Scudder's work involved several tasks that brought him into contact with insulation materials containing asbestos.As a maintenance helper, he sometimes drilled into insulated pipes and equipment to remove plugs. He also used a wrench to knock off pipe coverings. The court noted that these activities created dust.He helped insulation workers cut pipes and prepare insulating cement. Scudder estimated that he worked with insulation for about three hours a week. When he poured dry cement powder into a bucket and mixed it with water, it created visible dust.At other times, he helped clean insulation debris. He also spent about 15 minutes twice a week sweeping the insulation shop.Scudder told the court that before 1980, he did not recall receiving warnings about asbestos or training on how to handle it. He also did not remember being given a mask or respirator or seeing warning signs about asbestos at the refinery. He said he did not recall the refinery testing the air for asbestos.In 1989, he received a week's training on asbestos removal. He was taught about the risks, how to set up enclosed work areas and how to use protective clothing and a respirator. He was also shown how to collect and dispose of asbestos safely.Tyler MD argued that Scudder's exposure at the refinery was too low to have caused his mesothelioma. It pointed out that the exposure levels calculated for him were below the limits permitted under workplace safety standards at the time.The family's industrial hygiene expert, Kenneth Garza, reviewed Scudder's work history and testimony. He calculated his asbestos exposure between 1972 and 1980 at 0.175.
